instructions: Read the original passage and choose one answer for each question.
passage:
In the fictional town of Greenbank, a rescue group holds a Saturday meeting for people who may want an animal companion. The staff do not ask visitors to make an immediate decision. They invite them to talk about their homes, time and expectations first. A permanent home and a temporary stay are different commitments, and the right choice depends on the people and the individual animal.

Mara arrives on Saturday at two in the afternoon with her friend Dev. She is interested in an adult cat named Miso. The staff explain that Miso was found as a stray cat and is staying with a volunteer for now. Mara could apply to adopt Miso, but she could also ask whether she is able to foster an animal for a limited period. The group asks every visitor to read its current information and discuss any questions with staff before deciding.

In another room, a puppy named Nell is resting near a blanket and a soft toy. Her collar has a tag with the center's name. When a door closes, she may bark, so the volunteer gives visitors time to listen before they come closer. Nell looks friendly with one familiar person but nervous when the room becomes noisy. The staff say that a first meeting shows only part of an animal's temperament. They do not promise that any animal will behave the same way in every setting.

Mara also sees a kitten, a rabbit and a bird in separate spaces. A worker points to a loose feather near the bird's cage and then to the kitten's fur. The rabbit moves its tail, while Nell lifts one paw beside her crate. These details help Mara learn the English words. The group does not ask visitors to handle the animals without a staff member. Mara listens to the worker's explanation and writes down which questions she still wants to ask.

Dev says he likes Nell, but he travels often and cannot promise a regular schedule. If he had more time, he would ask about a longer visit before making a decision. Mara thinks trust can take patience and that affection alone does not tell her which home is suitable. A gentle introduction and honest questions may help the staff understand each visitor's situation. At the end of the meeting, the team offers visitors a blank sheet for their questions. They can take it home, think about what they learned and contact the center for current information. No one is asked to decide before leaving. Mara decides to talk with them again the following week; she does not sign an adoption form that day. The story is invented for language practice and is not a substitute for advice from the people responsible for an actual animal.
